readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: confessions and horrid little houses (Chapter I, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how the adult Addams explains her childhood feelings without mocking them, and which memories she chooses to begin a life’s work.
readings.focus: A memoir that traces a public vocation back to a child’s conscience, fears and love for her father.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Its first chapters recall her childhood in the Illinois village of Cedarville, where her father, John Addams, owned a flour mill and a sawmill and served in the state senate. Her mother died when she was two, and a childhood illness left her with a curved spine. A newel post stands at the foot of a staircase; the Second Adventists expected the world to end soon; bran and shorts are by-products of milling flour; the mill-race is the channel that brings water to the mill-wheel. Some phrases she quotes come from poems, among them Wordsworth’s ode on childhood (“the fields of sleep”).
readings.contentNote: Contains a young child’s terror of death and Hell, and her shame about her looks and her curved spine.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Earliest Impressions,” from the opening through the mills across the road; opens “ON the theory that our genuine impulses may be connected with our childish experiences,…”; closes “…us wet the edges of the pile with water brought in his sprinkling pot from the mill-race.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the child creep down to her father’s room after telling a lie, and why does his answer comfort her even though he grants no “absolution”?
facilitatorNotes: She fears dying in her sin and fears that her father, standing for the whole adult world she has deceived, might die before she confesses. He neither scolds nor forgives: he says he is glad a little girl who told lies felt too bad to sleep. He approves her conscience rather than judging the lie, and knowing that her wickedness is “shared” lets her sleep.
evidence: No absolution was asked for or received
at least that of the comforted

questions.prompt: At about six she declares she will build her house “right in the midst of horrid little houses.” Why might Addams put this memory near the start of her memoir, and how far should a reader trust it?
facilitatorNotes: It points straight at Hull-House, founded among the poor. But the memoir’s first sentence admits a “theory” that childish experiences explain adult impulses, and a writer looking back chooses memories that fit the life she lived. Readers can treat it as evidence of an early calling, or as a memory shaped by what came later; the text supports both.
evidence: the theory that our genuine impulses may be connected with our childish experiences
right in the midst of horrid little houses like those

questions.prompt: In the wagon-wheel dream and on the Sunday walks with Uncle James, the child carries burdens nobody asked her to carry. What do the two memories share, and what ends the second one?
facilitatorNotes: Both are secret duties she imagines for herself: to restart the world single-handed, and to protect her handsome father from being linked with his “Ugly Duckling” daughter. Neither is confided to anyone. Her father ends the second without knowing it by bowing to her in the street with his silk hat, a public sign that he is glad to be known as hers.
evidence: upon me rested the responsibility of making a wagon wheel
With a playful touch of exaggeration, he lifted his high and shining silk hat and made me an imposing bow.

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a miller’s thumb and a new cloak (Chapter I, second part)
readings.challenge: Compare what her father says in each conversation with what the child hoped he would say.
readings.focus: Lessons in equality and honesty, taught more by example and by refusal than by instruction.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Its first chapters recall her childhood in the Illinois village of Cedarville, where her father, John Addams, owned a flour mill and a sawmill and served in the state senate. Her mother died when she was a baby, and her father remarried when she was eight. To dress millstones is to recut their grinding grooves with a chisel; to bolt flour is to sift it. A self-made man is one who rose from poverty by his own work. Foreordination (predestination) is the doctrine that God has decided in advance who will be saved; the shorter catechism is a book of questions and answers on Christian belief. Hicksite Quakers were the more liberal branch of the Society of Friends after it split in 1827.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Earliest Impressions,” from the mill and her father’s habits through “I am a Hicksite Quaker”; opens “In addition to these fascinations was the association of the mill with my father's…”; closes “…Quaker"; and not another word on the weighty subject could I induce him to utter.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the child want a flattened thumb and spotted hands? What does the adult Addams make of this “tribute of imitation”?
facilitatorNotes: They were the marks of her father’s years as a miller’s apprentice, and she wanted to share the hardships of his early life; she even wakes at three, as he does, and resolves to read his books. The adult calls the imitation genuine affection, but also places it, a little drily, in her generation’s admiration for “the self-made man.”
evidence: I believe I have never since wanted anything more desperately than I wanted my right thumb to be flattened
that stream of admiration which our generation so generously poured forth for the self-made man

questions.prompt: Her father advises her to wear her old cloak. Does she agree? What does his answer about equality claim, and what does it leave unsolved?
facilitatorNotes: She obeys “without inner consent.” He says people may never be equal in clothes but can be equal in what matters more, school and church, so it is foolish to dress in a way that makes even that equality harder. The deeper problem, “the inequalities of the human lot,” is left standing; readers may find his answer wise, practical, or too easy for a wealthy man to give.
evidence: I complied with the request but I fear without inner consent
it was very stupid to wear the sort of clothes that made it harder to have equality even there

questions.prompt: Asked about foreordination, her father admits he does not understand it either; asked what he is, he says only “I am a Quaker.” What is he teaching by what he declines to say?
facilitatorNotes: Honesty with oneself: never pretend to understand what you do not, and keep “mental integrity above everything else.” His short answer about his faith, with its one joking addition, values conviction over doctrine and labels. The child is thrilled to be treated as his equal in not understanding; readers may notice that the lesson is taught by example, not by argument.
evidence: it was very important not to pretend to understand what you didn't understand
mental integrity above everything else

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: Polly’s death, and Mazzini’s (Chapter I, end)
readings.challenge: Follow how each memory leads Addams to a general claim, and test each claim against the memory behind it.
readings.focus: A country childhood, a first encounter with death, and the discovery that a stranger abroad can be mourned.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Its first chapters recall her childhood in the Illinois village of Cedarville, where her father, John Addams, owned a flour mill and a sawmill and served in the state senate. Hawthorne’s story “Ethan Brand” is about a lime-burner who seeks the unpardonable sin; a limekiln is a furnace for turning limestone into lime. The Vulgate is the Latin Bible. Giuseppe Mazzini (1805–1872) was an Italian patriot who worked for a free, united Italy, then partly ruled by the Austrian Habsburgs (spelled Hapsburg here). A doublet is a man’s close-fitting jacket; the closing lines are from Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s verse novel Aurora Leigh.
readings.contentNote: Contains a death witnessed by a fifteen-year-old, and children killing snakes for a pretend sacrifice.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Earliest Impressions,” from the scene of rural beauty to the end of the chapter; opens “These early recollections are set in a scene of rural beauty, unusual at least for…”; closes “"He wrapt me in his large Man's doublet, careless did it fit or no."”.

questions.prompt: Addams contrasts her long country games with the play of city children near Hull-House. What is her argument, and what in her own childhood supports it?
facilitatorNotes: Country children could keep a game going “summer after summer”; city children’s play is constantly broken up by traffic until they give up and stand around. Her altar beside the stream, used for years, shows the continuity she means. Readers may ask whether she romanticises the country, and whether her own unusual freedom was typical.
evidence: as only free-ranging country children can do
the constant interruption to their play which is inevitable on the streets

questions.prompt: How does Polly’s death change the way the fifteen-year-old sees the world, and what does Addams conclude about how adults should treat the young?
facilitatorNotes: The dying woman calls her by her mother’s name, and the familiar face becomes “strange, august”; Jane feels “unsheltered” and rides home full of questions about the journey of the dead. She concludes that children should not be shielded from death and sorrow, because they want to share the “common human experiences.” Readers can debate how far her claim holds for every child.
evidence: of being unsheltered in a wide world of relentless and elemental forces
They too wish to climb steep stairs and to eat their bread with tears

questions.prompt: The child argues that her father did not even know Mazzini, who “was not an American.” What does she learn, and why might this memory belong in the memoir of someone who worked among immigrants?
facilitatorNotes: That people who share large hopes are truly related, whatever their nation, language or creed, and that her patriotism had been “meager.” At Hull-House she would live among neighbours from many countries; the memory explains the international sympathy she brought there. The closing lines from Aurora Leigh turn the lesson back to her father, who “wrapt” her in ideas too large for her yet.
evidence: even though they differ in nationality, language, and creed
I was heartily ashamed of my meager notion of patriotism

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: flags on the gateposts and Old Abe (Chapter II, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how stories of the war reached the children, and how Addams separates griefs that have causes from griefs that have none.
readings.focus: The Civil War as a child knew it: rosters, local heroes, unexplained losses, and a symbol under a dome.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Its first chapters recall her childhood in the Illinois village of Cedarville, where her father, John Addams, owned a flour mill and a sawmill and served in the state senate. She was four when Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865. The roster on the family wall lists a local company of Union volunteers, “Addams’ Guard.” Fort Donelson, in Tennessee, was a Union victory in 1862; Andersonville was a Confederate prison camp in Georgia where thousands of Union prisoners died. Old Abe was a bald eagle carried into battle by the 8th Wisconsin Regiment and kept afterwards in the state capitol at Madison. Walter Pater was an English critic; an ensign is a banner.
readings.contentNote: Contains soldiers’ deaths from wounds and in prison, a young man killed in a hunting accident, and grieving parents.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Influence of Lincoln,” from Lincoln’s death through the visit to the war eagle; opens “I SUPPOSE all the children who were born about the time of the Civil War have…”; closes “…as the eagle had been the ensign of courage to the soldiers of the Wisconsin regiment.”.

questions.prompt: How did the war reach the Addams children? Gather the objects and stories, and say what each taught them about heroism.
facilitatorNotes: The flags with black on the gateposts and her father’s first tears; the roster, read by standing on the Bible and the dictionary; the picture of the one-armed colonel; Tommy’s mother and her son’s refusal to be smuggled out of hospital. Heroism came to them as local names, family grief and a soldier’s pride, not as battles.
evidence: To my amazement I found my father in tears, something that I had never seen before
No, sir; I will go out of the front door or I'll die here.

questions.prompt: Why do the children fall silent at the old couple’s farmhouse? What difference does Addams draw between that grief and others?
facilitatorNotes: Five sons enlisted, only the youngest came home, and he was killed by accident on the farm that autumn. No one is to blame: it is “the grief of things as they are,” harder to bear than griefs we can trace to wrongdoing. She says she later needed this early sense of “mysterious injustice,” presumably in her work among the poor.
evidence: that grief of things as they are, so much more mysterious and intolerable than those griefs which we think dimly to trace to man's own wrongdoing
that mysterious injustice, the burden of which we are all forced to bear

questions.prompt: The trip was made to see the eagle, but the “crowning moment” came under the capitol dome. What did the dome mean to the child, and why does the adult connect it with Lincoln?
facilitatorNotes: The dome enclosed ideas too vast for her (soldiers dying for freedom, pioneers founding a state) in a space “small enough for my child’s mind.” As the eagle had been the soldiers’ ensign of courage, Lincoln became the “standard bearer” of conscience. Addams’s point is that children grasp symbols before they grasp facts; readers may ask what such symbols leave out.
evidence: children are as quick to catch the meaning of a symbol as they are unaccountably slow to understand the real world about them
the martyred President as the standard bearer to the conscience of his countrymen

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: Mr. Lincoln’s letters and a refused bribe (Chapter II, middle)
readings.challenge: Trace how Addams measures her own conduct against her father’s, and how her idea of a hero changes.
readings.focus: Integrity in public life, and a turn from great men to the people themselves.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Its first chapters recall her childhood in the Illinois village of Cedarville, where her father, John Addams, owned a flour mill and a sawmill and served in the state senate. Her father served in the Illinois state senate from 1854 to 1870 and knew Abraham Lincoln there. In the summer of 1894 a strike against the Pullman railway-car company spread through Chicago, and the President sent federal troops over the protest of the governor of Illinois; Augustus Saint-Gaudens’s statue of Lincoln stands in Chicago’s Lincoln Park. A sweatshop bill was a proposed law regulating crowded workshops; a Te Deum is a hymn of thanksgiving; Thomas Carlyle’s On Heroes and Hero-Worship argued that history is made by great men; Carl Schurz was a German-American statesman who wrote an essay on Lincoln.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Influence of Lincoln,” from the honorary degree at Wisconsin through Old Settlers’ Day and the copies of Schurz’s Lincoln; opens “Thirty-five years later, as I stood on the hill campus of the University of Wisconsin…”; closes “…boys twenty-five copies of the then new Carl Schurz's "Appreciation of Abraham Lincoln."”.

questions.prompt: Lincoln’s letter asks which way “Double-D'ed” Addams’s conscience was pointing. What do the letter and the newspaper tribute after his death say about her father’s reputation?
facilitatorNotes: Lincoln trusted him to vote by conscience and only asked which way it pointed. The editor’s tribute goes further: bad men never offered him a bribe because they were afraid of him. His honesty was so plain that it prevented corruption rather than resisting it.
evidence: My dear Double-D'ed Addams
had never been offered a bribe because bad men were instinctively afraid of him

questions.prompt: When manufacturers offer fifty thousand dollars to drop the sweatshop bill, why does Addams blame herself as well as them? How does she handle the moment?
facilitatorNotes: Remembering her father, she reasons that no one would have offered her a bribe unless they saw some weakness in her. She refuses gently, with a youthful flourish about singing a Te Deum on the ruins of Hull-House, and the company hurries past the awkwardness. Readers may admire her self-examination or think the self-blame misplaced, since the offer says more about the givers.
evidence: it could not have occurred unless a weakness in myself had permitted it
that scurrying away from ugly morality which seems to be an obligation of social intercourse

questions.prompt: Why does Carlyle’s book about heroes stop convincing the young Addams on Old Settlers’ Day? What takes its place?
facilitatorNotes: An old farm woman who had bought railway stock “out of butter and egg money” calls out that she would do it again, and her father presents her gravely as a public-spirited pioneer. Heroism now seems to belong to ordinary people, as Lincoln understood; years later she gives a boys’ club Schurz’s Lincoln instead of Carlyle. Readers can ask whether Lincoln himself is not still a great-man hero in her account.
evidence: the people themselves were the great resource of the country
I'm here to-day, Mr. Addams, and I'd do it again if you asked me.

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: Lincoln at Oxford (Chapter II, end)
readings.challenge: Follow Addams’s unease at Oxford, and notice how one remembered phrase resolves it.
readings.focus: Democracy against class: an American settlement worker tests an English idea against her own country.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. The settlement movement began in London, where Toynbee Hall (1884) was founded so that university men could live among the poor of the East End; Arnold Toynbee, T. H. Green, John Ruskin and others inspired it, and Ruskin once set Oxford students to mend a country road. Edward Caird, Master (head) of Balliol College, Oxford, wrote The Evolution of Religion; Benjamin Jowett was an earlier Master. Sangamon County, Illinois, was Lincoln’s home district. “The pit whence they were digged” echoes the Bible (Isaiah 51:1) and means one’s origins. The idea that a country can be “two nations,” rich and poor, comes from a novel by Benjamin Disraeli, later Britain’s prime minister.
readings.contentNote: Addams writes as an educated reformer about immigrant families; her assumptions about class and about immigrants’ children are kept as written for critical reading.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Influence of Lincoln,” from Lincoln at early Hull-House to the end of the chapter; opens “In our early effort at Hull-House to hand on to our neighbors whatever of help we had…”; closes “…remains the most valuable contribution America has made to the moral life of the world.”.

questions.prompt: What does Addams tell immigrant children about Lincoln, and why does she think they need to hear it?
facilitatorNotes: Some children of immigrants are ashamed of their parents’ language and customs and count success as forgetting the past. She holds up Lincoln, who never forgot how the plain people of Sangamon County thought, as proof that keeping one’s past is the root of growth. Readers may weigh whether this respects the children or lectures them.
evidence: who were ashamed of the pit whence they were digged
his marvelous power to retain and utilize past experiences

questions.prompt: Why does the English movement seem “involved and roundabout” to her, and why does she feel she is “playing two rôles at once”?
facilitatorNotes: She believes pioneer life in the rural West made social distinctions impossible, so Oxford students mending a road out of principle look odd when American citizens mend their roads every spring, although she remembers, uneasily, being stuck in those roads. Part of her admires English social thought; another part, the “rustic American,” looks on sceptically. Readers can test her claim that her America had no classes.
evidence: where the early pioneer life had made social distinctions impossible
that uncomfortable sense of playing two rôles at once

questions.prompt: Caird’s description of Lincoln as one “content merely to dig the channels” settles her unease. What does the image mean, and how does it connect with her argument about the word “settlement”?
facilitatorNotes: A leader prepares channels through which other people’s moral life can flow; settlement workers likewise “dig channels” so that justice can reach “the barren places of life.” She rejects the English assumption of a superior class with duties to an inferior one and claims democracy, mistakes and all, as America’s gift. Some readers will note the tension between that claim and her own position as a well-off benefactor.
evidence: who was content merely to dig the channels through which the moral life of his countrymen might flow
We do not like to acknowledge that Americans are divided into two nations

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a fever of preparation (Chapter III, first part)
readings.challenge: Notice how the adult Addams smiles at her schoolgirl self, and what she still takes seriously.
readings.focus: Ardent young women in a school built on sacrifice, hungry for experience and resisting religious pressure.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. In 1877, at seventeen, Addams entered Rockford Female Seminary in Illinois, a school for women modelled on Mount Holyoke in Massachusetts, which trained many missionaries; Smith College was a new women’s college in the East. Thomas De Quincey’s Confessions of an English Opium-Eater describes the dreams opium gave him; an emetic makes a person vomit. Bellerophon is the Greek hero who rode the winged horse Pegasus to kill the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster. Plutarch wrote lives of famous Greeks and Romans; Motley and Gibbon wrote very long histories. Evangelical appeals urged students to declare a personal conversion; the Port Royalists were a seventeenth-century French community devoted to learning, piety and manual work; Plato’s Crito shows Socrates in prison before his death. Her father died in August 1881, after she left school.
readings.contentNote: Contains a group of students secretly taking opium as an experiment, and grief after a parent’s death.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Boarding-School Ideals,” from her arrival at Rockford through Professor Blaisdell’s gift of the Crito; opens “AS my three older sisters had already attended the seminary at Rockford, of which my…”; closes “…of literature from which the donor himself had drawn waters of healing and inspiration.”.

questions.prompt: What was the “fever of preparation” at Rockford, and how does the older Addams regard it?
facilitatorNotes: The first students, aware of the founders’ sacrifices, felt every minute must be used; later girls inherited the intensity “without knowing that it could have been otherwise.” Addams quotes the grim Aristotle on the club wall and her group’s complaint that preparation and routine left no room for “any experience at all” with amused affection, gently mocking an earnestness she still respects.
evidence: a fever of preparation which continued long after the direct making of it had ceased
we find it difficult to have any experience at all

questions.prompt: Why did five students take opium, and how does Addams tell the story? What does it show about the girls?
facilitatorNotes: To understand De Quincey’s “Dreams” “more sympathetically.” Nothing happened except suspense; a young teacher took the powders away, gave each an emetic and sent them to evening worship “whether we were able to or not.” Addams tells it as comedy, mocking the “aspirants for sympathetic understanding of all human experience,” but it shows how hungry the girls were for real experience, and how reckless that hunger could be.
evidence: by drugging ourselves with opium
the five aspirants for sympathetic understanding of all human experience

questions.prompt: Addams resisted every appeal to convert, yet found “the beauty of holiness” in Sunday readings of the Gospels in Greek, and comfort after her father’s death in sorrow as “the common lot.” What kind of religion does she value, and what kind does she resist?
facilitatorNotes: She resists emotional pressure, compulsory prayer meetings, doctrine and Gospels “cut up into chapter and verse.” She values quiet reading of whole Gospels without argument, in a clean room, with freedom of translation, and a consolation that turns her grief outward toward everyone’s sorrow rather than inward in “resignation.” Her father’s independent morality shaped this. Readers may call it faith, or an ethical humanism that would serve her at Hull-House.
evidence: I was singularly unresponsive to all these forms of emotional appeal
This realization of sorrow as the common lot, of death as the universal experience, was the first comfort which my bruised spirit had received.

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: fifth place, and the perils of self-tradition (Chapter III, end)
readings.challenge: Follow how Addams tests her schoolgirl ideals against what came later, and where she admits she was wrong.
readings.focus: Ideals formed at school, and the slow, uncertain work of turning them into justice.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. Rockford Seminary was working to become a college that could grant degrees, which it did in 1882. The franchise is the right to vote; “Woman’s Cause” was the movement for women’s rights. William Jennings Bryan, a fellow student orator, later became famous for his “Cross of Gold” speech (1896) and ran three times for President. A coign of vantage is a good position from which to act; the single tax was a proposed tax on land values alone; Sombart and Loria were economists. Arbitrators settle a dispute that both sides agree to accept; a union shop employs only union members. Cassandra, in Greek legend, foretold the truth and was never believed. Darwin’s Origin of Species (1859) set out the theory of evolution; Butler’s Analogy was a defence of Christian belief.
readings.contentNote: Contains the dated term “Deaf and Dumb” for deaf people and “crippled” for a disabled worker.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “Boarding-School Ideals,” from Rockford’s bid to become a college to the end of the chapter; opens “Throughout our school years, we were always keenly conscious of the growing development…”; closes “…and refusing to be content with a shadowy intellectual or aesthetic reflection of it.”.

questions.prompt: How do Addams’s classmates treat her as the college’s first orator, and how does she tell the story of the contest and its aftermath?
facilitatorNotes: They criticize her with “brutal frankness,” especially her “feminine, apologetic” habit of dropping her voice. She places fifth, behind Bryan among others, then delays her return to visit the state institutions and finds her friends’ garlands drooping and their judgment stern: she has dealt Woman’s Cause “a staggering blow.” She tells it with mock-heroic humour (“our field of Waterloo”), laughing at youthful seriousness, her own included.
evidence: which would probably lose Woman the first place
I had dealt the cause of woman's advancement a staggering blow

questions.prompt: Addams calls her schoolgirl oration on Justice “premature pragmatism,” yet says she still believes it. What does it claim, and how does the arbitration case test it?
facilitatorNotes: Justice comes not by longing, a millennium or a hero, but “by trained intelligence, by broadened sympathies toward the individual,” one case at a time. The arbitration over a disabled non-union worker shows how hard that is: old evidence cannot be trusted, resentment is ten years deep, and the arbitrators labour for “the inner consent of all concerned.” She admits she is not sure they did justice, but concludes that justice in industry needs the same patience as civic justice. Readers may weigh whether this patient method is wisdom or too slow for urgent wrongs.
evidence: The actual Justice must come by trained intelligence
I am not quite sure that in the end we administered justice

questions.prompt: The graduates warned each other against losing their “early ideals.” What did they fail to foresee, and what does the chapter’s ending admit about Addams herself?
facilitatorNotes: They expected the danger to be giving up their ideals; they did not foresee “the obscure paths of tolerance, just allowance, and self-blame” through which real understanding comes. Addams admits she spent eight years “absolutely at sea” before founding Hull-House. The chapter ends not in triumph but in honest uncertainty, which makes her later work seem earned rather than destined.
evidence: the obscure paths of tolerance, just allowance, and self-blame
I was absolutely at sea so far as any moral purpose was concerned

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a Saturday night in East London (Chapter IV, first part)
readings.challenge: Weigh a single overwhelming scene as evidence, and notice how Addams judges both what she saw and how she saw it.
readings.focus: A first sight of extreme poverty, and the discovery that a cultivated mind can get in the way of seeing it.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. After college Addams began medical training in Philadelphia, but illness ended it, and her doctor sent her to Europe for two years. Dr. S. Weir Mitchell was a Philadelphia physician known for prescribing long bed rest; Carlyle’s Frederick the Great is a long history and Gray’s Anatomy a medical textbook. Hucksters are street sellers; farthings and ha’pennies were the smallest English coins; the “submerged tenth” was a new phrase for the very poorest part of the population. Thomas De Quincey was an English essayist; “The Vision of Sudden Death” is part of his essay on a night ride on the mail-coach. The saying about “conduct” comes from the critic Matthew Arnold.
readings.contentNote: Describes starving people in London eating spoiled food. “Savagery,” used of humanity’s distant past, reflects period ideas of human progress.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Snare of Preparation,” from the opening through “conduct, and not culture”; opens “THE winter after I left school was spent in the Woman's Medical College of Philadelphia,…”; closes “…the moderns plainly said that "conduct, and not culture is three fourths of human life."”.

questions.prompt: Addams says she can recall these struggles only through notebooks written “only in moments of deep depression.” How should that affect the way we read the chapter? What other cause of her struggles does she admit?
facilitatorNotes: She warns that her record is lopsided: the notebooks catch her low points, not her ordinary days. She also concedes that her long illness and “nervous depression” lay behind much of it, though she insists it “could not have been all due to my health.” A memoirist who questions her own sources invites the reader to weigh them too.
evidence: only in moments of deep depression when overwhelmed by a sense of failure
doubtless there was much nervous depression at the foundation of the spiritual struggles which this chapter is forced to record

questions.prompt: In the Mile End Road scene, what details does Addams give first, and what is her “final impression”? Why might the hands stay with her for the rest of her life?
facilitatorNotes: She first notes clothing, pale faces and the “cunning” of people who must bargain or starve, and the man who eats a raw cabbage on the curb. What remains is “myriads of hands,” reaching for food already unfit to eat. Hands mean work and need at once, “this oldest tool” of human progress, which is why a classroom of raised hands still brings the scene back.
evidence: but of myriads of hands, empty, pathetic, nerveless and workworn
this oldest tool with which man has dug his way from savagery

questions.prompt: Addams calls what she saw “most fragmentary and lurid” and “quite unfair.” Unfair to whom? Why include the admission?
facilitatorNotes: Unfair to the many people already working among the poor, whom the tourists never saw, and perhaps to the poor themselves, shown to visitors as a spectacle by a guide pleased with a “new phrase.” She admits that a single vivid glimpse is weak evidence, even as she shows how strongly it shaped her. Readers can ask whether a scene can be unfair as evidence and still true as experience.
evidence: It was, of course, a most fragmentary and lurid view of the poverty of East London, and quite unfair.
I should have been shown either less or more

questions.prompt: Why does remembering De Quincey at that moment disgust her? Do you agree that literature “only served to cloud the really vital situation”?
facilitatorNotes: De Quincey, facing an accident, could not shout a warning until he had remembered a line of Homer; Addams, facing hunger, reached for De Quincey. She sees a “vicious circle” of educated people who respond to life through books. Yet she makes the point with a literary story and a quotation, in a memoir that is itself literature, so readers can argue that books may also sharpen what we see.
evidence: lumbering our minds with literature that only served to cloud the really vital situation spread before our eyes
conduct, and not culture is three fourths of human life

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a sweet dessert in the morning (Chapter IV, middle)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument about education that moves between general claims and particular scenes, and test the claims against the scenes.
readings.focus: Cultivation without purpose, a protest that changes nothing, and a search for fellowship.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. In the 1880s, after illness ended her medical training, Addams spent two years in Europe, where a night in the poorest part of London had shocked her into doubting the value of her studies. Weltschmerz (German) is world-weariness; pensions are boarding-houses; a Hausfrau is a housewife; Saxe-Coburg was a small German duchy; Baron Stockmar was tutor and adviser to Prince Albert, Queen Victoria’s husband; Albrecht Dürer was a German artist of the Reformation era, and St. Hubert is one of his engravings; the Roman Campagna is the countryside round Rome; the Catacombs are early Christian burial tunnels; Mazzini was a leader of Italian unification. “The great refusal” is Dante’s phrase for turning down a great calling. The two lines of verse open Matthew Arnold’s poem “Self-Dependence.”
readings.contentNote: Describes women scarred by scalding at work.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, from the “Weltschmerz” of educated young women through Addams’s joining the village church; opens “For two years in the midst of my distress over the poverty which, thus suddenly driven…”; closes “…be so easy for the world to slip back into the doctrines of selection and aristocracy?”.

questions.prompt: Addams argues that the first generation of college women had lost “that simple and almost automatic response to the human appeal.” What does she think their education did to them?
facilitatorNotes: It trained them to acquire knowledge and “receive impressions,” not to act, and kept them so sheltered that they were never asked to do anything, not even to refuse. Ask whether the criticism is of women’s education in particular or of any education that keeps students as spectators, and whether it still applies.
evidence: had developed too exclusively the power of acquiring knowledge and of merely receiving impressions
they are so sheltered and pampered they have no chance even to make "the great refusal."

questions.prompt: Compare the mother and the daughter in the pensions. What does the daughter want to cry out, and why can’t she say it?
facilitatorNotes: The mother bustles, talks bad German and makes real connections; the daughter sits “being cultivated.” The daughter knows she has fine chances and no real talent, and envies her mother’s busy girlhood full of obstacles. She cannot say so without sounding ungrateful and wounding her mother. Addams writes as if from inside the daughter; readers may suspect she is describing herself.
evidence: I am simply smothered and sickened with advantages.
It is like eating a sweet dessert the first thing in the morning.

questions.prompt: In Saxe-Coburg Addams crosses the square to protest. What happens, and why does the incident spoil the book she had been reading?
facilitatorNotes: The brewery owner receives her with “exasperating indifference,” and the innkeeper slips away; the protest changes nothing. But it changes how she reads: a tutor devoted to making “princely the mind of his prince” seems blind to the multitude, and she turns to Dürer because his pictures refuse a “smooth and cultivated view of life.” Readers can judge whether her protest was brave, naive or both.
evidence: Stung into action by one of those sudden indignations against cruel conditions which at times fill the young with unexpected energy
how could a good man, feeling so keenly his obligation

questions.prompt: Addams joined the village church at twenty-five. What reasons does she give, and how does the decision connect with her “devotion to the ideals of democracy”?
facilitatorNotes: She felt no emotional “conversion” but wanted “an outward symbol of fellowship” after many “piteous failures.” She saw early Christianity, “the faith of the fisherman and the slave,” as a protest against a world built for a privileged few. The same chapter laughs at her walk into Rome like a pilgrim, so readers can notice how she separates sincere conviction from youthful theatre.
evidence: I took upon myself the outward expressions of the religious life with all humility and sincerity

the faith of the fisherman and the slave had been boldly opposed to the accepted moral belief that the well-being of a privileged few might justly be built upon the ignorance and sacrifice of the many

readings.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House: a bullfight in Madrid (Chapter IV, end)
readings.challenge: Track the experiences that finally move Addams from study to action, and judge which one does the work.
readings.focus: Good motives without knowledge, a naive faith in authority, and a moment of self-disgust that becomes a plan.
readings.context: Jane Addams (1860–1935) founded Hull-House in 1889 in a crowded immigrant neighbourhood of Chicago. It was a settlement house, where educated residents lived among poor neighbours and offered clubs, classes and help; Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910) is her memoir. In her twenties, after illness ended her medical training, Addams spent years studying and travelling in Europe while doubting the value of culture cut off from action. Collateral is property pledged against a loan; a promissory note is a written promise to repay; satyrs are goat-legged figures of Greek myth. The London match girls struck in 1888 against low pay and “phossy jaw,” a disease of the jawbone caused by phosphorus in match factories. The Positivists followed the French philosopher Auguste Comte’s “religion of humanity.” Caparisoned horses wear ornamental coverings; a raison d’être is a reason for existing. Ellen Gates Starr, her school friend, later founded Hull-House with her. Toynbee Hall in East London was the first settlement house.
readings.contentNote: Describes starving hogs eating one of their own, children compared to animals, a disfiguring industrial disease, and a bullfight in which bulls and horses are killed. A streetcar conductor, quoted by Addams, uses the ethnic slur “dago” for Italian immigrants.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, from the drought-stricken farm to the end of the chapter; opens “In one of the intervening summers between these European journeys I visited a western…”; closes “…when they are longing to construct the world anew and to conform it to their own ideals.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Addams withdraw her mortgage money, and what does the sheep farm teach her about good motives?
facilitatorNotes: She cannot accept interest from farms that drought can reduce to such misery, though withdrawing causes “hardship to the farmers.” The sheep farm, meant to do good, ends in rotting hoofs because neither partner knew the work. Her own phrase, “the impeccability of her motives,” mocks the idea that meaning well is enough.
evidence: It seemed to me quite impossible to receive interest from mortgages placed upon farms which might at any season be reduced to such conditions
perhaps one partner depended too much upon the impeccability of her motives

questions.prompt: At the match girls’ meeting Addams did not connect what she saw with “the labor movement.” What did she still believe, according to her comparison with a young character of Wells’s?
facilitatorNotes: That somewhere a body of “authoritative people” would put things right once they knew; that the world might be tragic but never “contemptible or squalid or self-seeking.” Her search for a “cathedral of humanity” in Ulm and Comte belongs to the same hope. Her “smug notebook” shows the older writer smiling at it.
evidence: that somewhere in Church or State are a body of authoritative people who will put things to rights as soon as they really know what is wrong
it never for an instant occurs to him that it may be contemptible or squalid or self-seeking

questions.prompt: Why does the bullfight, rather than any scene of poverty, finally move her to act? What does she accuse herself of?
facilitatorNotes: She watched the killing with “comparative indifference” because romantic associations (knights, gladiators) covered it, and her shocked friends made her see this. That night she recognized the same habit in her life: a beautiful plan had become “a defense for continued idleness.” The ox-cart image turns noble self-image into plain self-seeking.
evidence: a mere paper reform had become a defense for continued idleness
I had been tied to the tail of the veriest ox-cart of self-seeking

questions.prompt: The chapter’s title comes from Tolstoy, found “years afterward.” What is “the snare of preparation,” and does the chapter prove it is a snare? Could more preparation have helped her?
facilitatorNotes: It is endless study and travel that keep the young from acting “at the very period of life when they are longing to construct the world anew.” Her years of culture and the bullfight support Tolstoy; but the sheep farm shows what action without knowledge costs, and her trip to Toynbee Hall is preparation of a practical kind. A strong answer distinguishes passive “receptivity” from learning by doing.
evidence: It is easy to become the dupe of a deferred purpose, of the promise the future can never keep
hopelessly entangling them in a curious inactivity
